paragraphs: A tower crane is the object that says construction from a mile away. A lattice mast, a horizontal jib with a trolley running along it, a counter jib with concrete blocks at the back and an operator cab at the join - the whole thing is balanced rather than braced, which is why the counterweight is so visibly large.

The mesh runs 989,799 polygons and 992,944 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and almost all of that count is the lattice: every member is real geometry, which is what lets the crane read correctly against a sky rather than turning into a grey smear.

A rigged build sits on this page at $129 for when the jib has to slew or the hook to move. The static model at $99 covers construction and city visualisation, property development marketing, skyline scenes, film and television, and games. On sale since 2015.

A suborbital spaceplane is built around one trick: the tail booms fold upward for reentry, turning the aircraft into a shuttlecock that stabilises itself without control input. That feathering mechanism is the vehicle's whole safety argument, and it gives the airframe its twin boom layout and its unusual proportions.
The mesh is efficient at 139,044 polygons and 143,101 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the boom hinges, the cabin windows and the rocket nozzle.

A rigged build sits on this page at $149, which is the one to take if the tail has to feather. The static model at $99 covers commercial spaceflight marketing, space tourism material, news and documentary graphics, education and games. On sale since 2022.

A distillery is a room full of copper. Pot stills with their swan neck lyne arms, washbacks, condensers and the pipework linking them are the whole visual identity of whisky production, and the copper is not decorative - it reacts with the spirit and changes the flavour, which is why nobody replaces it with steel.
The mesh is efficient at 55,407 polygons and 60,506 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, which suits equipment shown as part of a room rather than examined weld by weld.

At $99 it suits distillery and beverage industry visualisation, brand and heritage marketing, food and drink production presentation, visitor centre and museum material, and games. On sale since 2021.

A laboratory rat is one of the most recognisable animals in science communication, and its proportions matter: a long naked tail roughly as long as the body, prominent rounded ears, a blunt nose and pink extremities against white fur. Any of those wrong and the animal reads as a mouse or as a wild rat instead.

The mesh is light at 5,992 polygons and 6,186 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 15 texture maps - 14 at 4096x4096 and one at 1024x1024. That texture weight against a small mesh is exactly right for an animal whose realism is all in the fur and skin.
At $99 it suits laboratory and research visualisation, medical and pharmaceutical presentation, biology education material, science journalism, and games. On sale since 2016.

Adding a canopy changes what a dhow is for. A bare working boat carried cargo or divers; a boat with a shaded deck carries passengers, and that single addition turns a traditional hull into the tourist and pearl diving craft seen along the Gulf coast today. The frame and the fabric have to sit convincingly over the sheer of the hull.
The mesh is efficient at 75,918 polygons and 76,754 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the planking, the canopy frame and the deck fittings.
At $99 and built to StemCell specification, it suits Gulf tourism and heritage material, maritime and coastal visualisation, cultural presentation, film and television, and games. On sale since 2025.

A pair of hands at very different scales is a specific and much used image: an adult hand with an infant's beside or inside it, which appears constantly in healthcare, parenting, insurance and charity communication. Building both convincingly is difficult, because a baby's hand is not a small adult hand - the proportions and the fat pads are entirely different.

This collection supplies both, rigged and prepared for Cinema 4D, so the fingers articulate and the pose can be adjusted rather than accepted. Hands are the hardest part of any character rig, and having two working sets delivered is the whole value.
At $94 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits healthcare and parenting material, charity and insurance communication, advertising, motion graphics and games. On sale since 2026.

A flexible tripod is made of segmented ball joints that let each leg wrap around a branch, a railing or a post rather than standing on flat ground. Those segments are the entire object visually, and they have to be modelled as real repeated joints because the whole appeal of the product is that it bends.
The mesh is efficient at 77,987 polygons and 81,531 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with almost all of that count in the leg segments and the ball head.

A rigged build sits on this page at $19, which is the one to take if the legs have to be posed. The static model at $89 covers camera and photography accessory marketing, content creator and vlogging material, retail and e-commerce renders, and games. Built to CheckMate specification, on sale since 2025.

The business end of a shredder is the rotor: a heavy drum carrying hammers or cutters that turn at speed inside a reinforced chamber. Everything else on the machine - the feed hopper, the discharge, the drive motor and the frame - exists to serve it and to survive being near it.
The mesh runs 271,455 polygons and 288,982 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the rotor, the hopper mouth and the frame bracing where the machine is examined.

At $89 and built to StemCell specification, it suits recycling and waste industry visualisation, equipment marketing and catalogues, sustainability and circular economy presentation, industrial interiors and games. On sale since 2024.

A form fill seal machine turns a roll of film into filled sealed pouches in one continuous operation: the film unwinds, folds over a former, is sealed along the sides, filled from above and cut. Modelling it means showing that path, because a packaging machine without a visible film route is just an enclosure.
The mesh runs 206,154 polygons and 107,756 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the geometry in the film former, the sealing jaws and the frame.
At $89 it suits food and packaging industry visualisation, machinery marketing and catalogues, production line scenes, technical and training material, and games. On sale since 2024.

Tea is picked from the top of a hedge, which is why the harvester straddles the row rather than driving alongside it. The cutting head runs across the machine at the height of the plucking table, with a collection blower behind it, and the whole vehicle sits on narrow tracks or wheels that fit between the rows.
The mesh runs 479,657 polygons and 262,029 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and it arrives rigged so the cutting head and the running gear can be animated.

Two more rigged builds share this page at the same $89, prepared for Cinema 4D and for Maya. Aimed at agriculture and agritech visualisation, plantation and food supply presentation, equipment marketing, education and games. On sale since 2023.

Teddy bears carry a specific set of expectations: jointed limbs that rotate rather than bend, a slightly oversized head, a stitched muzzle and paw pads. Getting those conventions right is what makes a soft toy read as a teddy rather than as a stylised bear, and a collection gives the variety a nursery or a shop shelf actually needs.

The bears arrive rigged and prepared for Maya, which matters for a jointed toy: the limbs pivot at fixed points rather than deforming, and a rig built for organic bending would produce the wrong motion entirely.
At $89 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits toy and retail visualisation, children's and family advertising, nursery and interior renders, animation and games. On sale since 2025.

A bale wagon is a flat trailer with a purpose-built deck: rails to keep round bales from rolling off, a low bed so bales can be pushed on from a loader, and a chassis long enough to carry a full load out of a field. The frame is the whole machine, and this build shows it bare rather than loaded.
The mesh is efficient at 147,817 polygons and 170,289 vertices in quads and tris with mixed UV layout, with the geometry in the frame members, the axles and the rails.

At $79 and built to StemCell specification, it suits agriculture and farming visualisation, rural landscape scenes, agricultural machinery marketing, food supply presentation and games. On sale since 2026.

A belt loader is a conveyor on wheels that raises to meet an aircraft's cargo door, and the whole vehicle is arranged around that: a driver's position at the side, a long belt boom that lifts hydraulically, guard rails along it and a very short chassis so it can manoeuvre under a wing.

The mesh runs 255,564 polygons and 269,620 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, and ships with 44 texture maps - 29 at 4096x4096 and 15 at 2048x2048, which is a substantial budget for ground equipment and shows in the paint, the markings and the wear.

A rigged build sits on this page at $99 for when the belt has to raise. The static model at $79 covers airport ground handling visualisation, aviation services marketing, apron scenes, training material and games. On sale since 2017.

This rifle was designed around a new cartridge rather than adapted to one, which shows in the receiver proportions and the heavier bolt carrier. Externally it carries a folding side stock, a full length top rail, an ambidextrous control set and a barrel profile sized for a considerably higher chamber pressure than earlier service rifles.

The mesh runs 133,781 polygons and 135,614 vertices in quads and tris with non-overlapping UVs, with the density in the rail, the controls and the muzzle device where a weapon is examined in close-up.

At $79 and built to CheckMate specification, it suits military and defence visualisation, film and television armouries, games, training material and equipment presentation. Real-world scale is kept, so it fits a character rig. On sale since 2024.
